design_detail: Matters Arising (Nature Medicine 27:1689–1690, published online 11 October 2021) by three authors, responding to MAPP1 (Mitchell et al., 2021). Seven running-text paragraphs and 10 references, without methods or new data; a third page carries the author contributions and competing interests. Argues that calling MDMA-assisted therapy a breakthrough requires benchmarking against first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies (or testing in people who did not respond to them), patient-relevant outcomes, longer follow-up, larger safety samples and attention to therapy time and cost. Locators count paragraphs from the start of the text on each printed page.
can_establish: What the authors argue about how MAPP1 should be benchmarked, and which comparison figures they cite for it.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy is more or less effective, safe or cost-effective than trauma-focused psychotherapies: the letter adds no data and compares effect sizes and remission rates across trials with different comparators and populations.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The study discussed is MAPP1, 90 adults with severe PTSD.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the authors chose the comparison sources (two guidelines, three meta-analyses, two trials and one narrative review).
sample.selection_effects: The psychotherapy effect sizes cited are against wait-list, usual care or other controls in other populations (including complex PTSD and female rape survivors), and the remission figures come from cognitive-therapy trials and a meta-analysis of CBT (described by the letter as for PTSD; its reference title names adult anxiety disorders); no evidence on psychotherapy outcomes in people like MAPP1's participants (severe, chronic, comorbid PTSD, nearly all with earlier therapy) is cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The letter describes MAPP1's therapy: three 90-minute preparatory sessions, three 8-hour MDMA sessions each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions, two therapists throughout (p. 1689, 6th paragraph).

comparison.controls: The letter's benchmark: first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR, trauma-focused CBT), compared through effect sizes and remission rates from other trials.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: standardized mean differences on PTSD symptoms; remission or loss of diagnosis; adverse effects; therapy time; cost-effectiveness.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the letter does not discuss MAPP1's blinding.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Cited (p. 1689): MAPP1 SMD 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37); sertraline 0.51 (0.38 to 0.64), paroxetine 0.36 (0.28 to 0.49) and trauma-focused psychotherapies 0.83 (0.69 to 0.97) against control (Lee et al., 2016); EMDR 2.07 (1.44 to 2.70) and trauma-focused CBT 1.46 (1.05 to 1.87) against wait-list (Mavranezouli et al., 2020); in complex PTSD against usual care, CBT 0.90 (0.68 to 1.11), exposure 1.05 (0.58 to 1.52) and EMDR 1.26 (interval printed as 0.512.01) (Karatzias et al., 2019); post-treatment remission of about 46% to over 70% with two versions of cognitive therapy (Ehlers et al., 2014) and about 53% (45% to 61%) in a meta-analysis the letter describes as of CBT for PTSD (its reference title, Springer et al., 2018, names adult anxiety disorders); at long-term follow-up only 22.2% (cognitive processing therapy) and 17.5% (prolonged exposure) still had a diagnosis (Resick et al., 2012).
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter cites MAPP1's 33% remission (MDMA arm, completers) but not its 67% loss of diagnosis or the placebo arm's 5% remission, and sets MAPP1's effect against an active control beside psychotherapy effects against wait-list or usual care.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A methodological argument: a breakthrough claim needs comparison with first-line psychotherapies or tests in people who did not respond to them, patient-relevant outcomes, mid- and long-term follow-up, and larger, longer safety evaluation; the supporting figures come from other trials and populations. The editors' check of the therapy time is consistent: 3 × 90 + 3 × 480 + 9 × 90 minutes = 2,520 minutes, equal to 28 sessions of 90 or 42 of 60 minutes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter says psychological interventions “attain similar or elevated symptom reduction compared with that due to MDMA-assisted psychotherapy” and that remission rates are higher for several first-line treatments (p. 1689, 3rd and 4th paragraphs); both are cross-trial comparisons in which MAPP1's effect is relative to placebo plus the same intensive therapy, whereas the psychotherapy effects are relative to wait-list, usual care or other controls in different populations. It states that MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects are substantial even with limited use, citing one narrative review (p. 1689, 5th paragraph). It does not discuss MAPP1's blinding or expectancy, its adverse-event recording or its use of completer denominators.

timeline.event: Reply by the MAPP1 authors: comparison with psychotherapies is not part of a regulatory phase 3 programme; pragmatic studies should be done.
MAPP2 again compared MDMA with placebo plus the same therapy; no benchmark against a first-line psychotherapy.

replication.where_it_stands: The benchmark the letter asks for has not been done in the sources read: both phase 3 trials compared MDMA with placebo plus the same therapy, and Brett & Bynum (2025) found no randomized trial with a psychotherapy comparator.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests (Competing interests, third page of the PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, NTNU, and St. Olav's Hospital, Trondheim (Halvorsen); CHU Rennes, INSERM CIC 1414, University of Rennes (Naudet); Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, University of Pavia (Cristea). J.Ø.H. and I.A.C. conceptualized the arguments and J.Ø.H. wrote the first draft. None of the 10 references is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial comparing MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time, or testing it in people who did not respond to an adequate course of such therapy, with blinded assessment, quality of life and at least 12 months of follow-up.

domains.note: A letter; sources chosen by the authors, no search.

The cited meta-analyses and trials are not appraised, and the different control conditions and populations behind the effect sizes and remission rates are not discussed, although the comparison depends on them.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 10 references is by the authors.
The need for benchmarking is argued as principle; the statement that MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects are substantial even with limited use rests on one narrative review.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how MDMA-assisted therapy compares with first-line psychotherapies
domains.note: Under-represented: that MAPP1's comparison arm received the same intensive therapy; dropout and non-response with trauma-focused psychotherapies; and MAPP1's blinding problem, which bears on its effect size and is not raised.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domains. The letter is a clear statement of the benchmarking argument and can be cited for that argument and for its description of MAPP1's therapy time (which the editors' arithmetic confirms). Its comparative effect sizes and remission rates are cross-trial figures against different controls and should not be cited as evidence that psychotherapies are as effective as or more effective than MDMA-assisted therapy.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that a treatment labelled a breakthrough should be evaluated against first-line psychological interventions, or in prespecified subgroups of people who do not improve with them, because guidelines (American Psychological Association; NICE) recommend trauma-focused psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR, trauma-focused CBT) as first-line treatments for PTSD.

Comparative figures cited: MAPP1 SMD 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37), which MAPP1 contrasted with the modest effects of medicines, given here from a meta-analysis (Lee et al., 2016) as sertraline 0.51 (0.38 to 0.64) and paroxetine 0.36 (0.28 to 0.49), with trauma-focused psychotherapies at 0.83 (0.69 to 0.97) against control in the same meta-analysis; EMDR 2.07 (1.44 to 2.70) and trauma-focused CBT 1.46 (1.05 to 1.87) against wait-list; in complex PTSD against usual care, CBT 0.90 (0.68 to 1.11), exposure 1.05 (0.58 to 1.52) and EMDR 1.26.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Remission: against MAPP1's 33% post-treatment remission, the letter cites about 46% to over 70% for two versions of cognitive therapy, about 53% (95% CI 45% to 61%) in a meta-analysis of CBT, and long-term follow-up in which 22.2% (cognitive processing therapy) and 17.5% (prolonged exposure) of an intent-to-treat sample of female rape survivors still had the diagnosis.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: the 22.2% and 17.5% of Resick et al. still meeting criteria mean 77.8% and 82.5% without the diagnosis at long-term follow-up in an intent-to-treat sample; the like-for-like MAPP1 figure is loss of diagnosis (61% of the dosed MDMA arm, by the editors' calculation), not its 33% remission among completers.

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects: serious adverse effects of MDMA were rare in MAPP1, but rare events are hard to evaluate in small phase 3 trials without long-term follow-up; citing one review, the authors call MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects substantial even with limited use and ask regulators to rely on more than a single small study for a post-approval risk-management plan.

Therapy time: MAPP1's psychotherapy amounted to the equivalent of 28 sessions of 90 minutes or 42 of 60 minutes, with two therapists in every session, against 8 to 16 sessions of 60 to 90 minutes with one therapist (or up to 20 hours) for first-line psychotherapies, half or less.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 3 × 90 + 3 × 480 + 9 × 90 = 2,520 minutes, which is 28 × 90 and 42 × 60.

key_findings.finding: What the authors ask for: a phase 3 programme with large pragmatic studies and adequate comparators such as trauma-focused psychotherapies, or tests in rigorously prespecified subgroups who did not respond to adequate courses of them; patient-relevant outcomes such as quality of life; mid- and long-term follow-up; and safety investigation in larger samples over longer periods.
The authors declare no competing interests.

reporting_issues.issue: The confidence interval for EMDR in complex PTSD is printed as 0.512.01, without a separator (presumably 0.51 to 2.01).

The remission comparison sets MAPP1's 33% (14 of 42 completers on MDMA, its strictest outcome) against figures from other populations and definitions, including a meta-analysis that the letter describes as of CBT for PTSD but whose title (reference 8, Springer et al., 2018) concerns adult anxiety disorders, so whether its 53% is a PTSD figure cannot be checked from the letter.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot show that remission is higher with first-line psychotherapies in people like MAPP1's participants.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says the cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy had not yet been formally evaluated, although MAPP1 itself cites a 2020 cost-effectiveness analysis (its reference 11) and the trial authors' reply says an evaluation based on the phase 3 design was under review.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not to be cited for the absence of economic evaluations.
